Bringing cinnamon to Europe
Cinnamon is a sweet, fragrant spice produced from the inner bark of trees of the genus
Cinnamomum, which is native to the Indian sub-continent. It was known in biblical times,
and is mentioned in several books of the Bible, both as an ingredient that was mixed
with oils for anointing people’s bodies, and also as a token indicating friendship among
lovers and friends. In ancient Rome, mourners attending funerals burnt cinnamon to
create a pleasant scent. Most often, however, the spice found its primary use as an
additive to food and drink. In the Middle Ages, Europeans who could afford the spice
used it to flavour food, particularly meat, and to impress those around them with their
ability to purchase an expensive condiment from the ‘exotic’ East. At a banquet, a host
would offer guests a plate with various spices piled upon it as a sign of the wealth at his
or her disposal. Cinnamon was also reported to have health benefits, and was thought
to cure various ailments, such as indigestion.
Toward the end of the Middle Ages, the European middle classes began to desire
the lifestyle of the elite, including their consumption of spices. This led to a growth in
demand for cinnamon and other spices. At that time, cinnamon was transported by Arab
merchants, who closely guarded the secret of the source of the spice from potential
rivals. They took it from India, where it was grown, on camels via an overland route
to the Mediterranean. Their journey ended when they reached Alexandria. European
traders sailed there to purchase their supply of cinnamon, then brought it back to Venice.
The spice then travelled from that great trading city to markets all around Europe.
Because the overland trade route allowed for only small quantities of the spice to reach
Europe, and because Venice had a virtual monopoly of the trade, the Venetians could
set the price of cinnamon exorbitantly high. These prices, coupled with the increasing
demand, spurred the search for new routes to Asia by Europeans eager to take part in
the spice trade.
Seeking the high profits promised by the cinnamon market, Portuguese traders arrived
on the island of Ceylon in the Indian Ocean toward the end of the 15th century. Before
Europeans arrived on the island, the state had organized the cultivation of cinnamon.
People belonging to the ethnic group called the Salagama would peel the bark off
young shoots of the cinnamon plant in the rainy season, when the wet bark was
more pliable. During the peeling process, they curled the bark into the ‘stick’ shape
still associated with the spice today. The Salagama then gave the finished product to
the king as a form of tribute. When the Portuguese arrived, they needed to increase

population, forcing them to work in cinnamon harvesting. In 1518, the Portuguese built
a fort on Ceylon, which enabled them to protect the island, so helping them to develop a
monopoly in the cinnamon trade and generate very high profits. In the late 16th century,
for example, they enjoyed a tenfold profit when shipping cinnamon over a journey of
eight days from Ceylon to India.
When the Dutch arrived off the coast of southern Asia at the very beginning of the
17th century, they set their sights on displacing the Portuguese as kings of cinnamon.
The Dutch allied themselves with Kandy, an inland kingdom on Ceylon. In return
for payments of elephants and cinnamon, they protected the native king from the
Portuguese. By 1640, the Dutch broke the 150-year Portuguese monopoly when they
overran and occupied their factories. By 1658, they had permanently expelled the
Portuguese from the island, thereby gaining control of the lucrative cinnamon trade.
In order to protect their hold on the market, the Dutch, like the Portuguese before them,

satisfy Europe’s ever-increasing appetite for cinnamon, the Dutch began to alter the
harvesting practices of the Ceylonese. Over time, the supply of cinnamon trees on the
island became nearly exhausted, due to systematic stripping of the bark. Eventually, the
Dutch began cultivating their own cinnamon trees to supplement the diminishing number

Then, in 1796, the English arrived on Ceylon, thereby displacing the Dutch from their

Oxytocin
The positive and negative effects of the chemical known as the ‘love hormone’
A
Oxytocin is a chemical, a hormone produced in the pituitary gland in the brain. It
was through various studies focusing on animals that scientists first became aware
of the influence of oxytocin. They discovered that it helps reinforce the bonds
between prairie voles, which mate for life, and triggers the motherly behaviour
that sheep show towards their newborn lambs. It is also released by women in
childbirth, strengthening the attachment between mother and baby. Few chemicals
have as positive a reputation as oxytocin, which is sometimes referred to as the
‘love hormone’. One sniff of it can, it is claimed, make a person more trusting,
empathetic, generous and cooperative. It is time, however, to revise this wholly
optimistic view. A new wave of studies has shown that its effects vary greatly
depending on the person and the circumstances, and it can impact on our social
interactions for worse as well as for better.
B
Oxytocin’s role in human behaviour first emerged in 2005. In a groundbreaking
experiment, Markus Heinrichs and his colleagues at the University of Freiburg,
Germany, asked volunteers to do an activity in which they could invest money with
an anonymous person who was not guaranteed to be honest. The team found
that participants who had sniffed oxytocin via a nasal spray beforehand invested
more money than those who received a placebo instead. The study was the start
of research into the effects of oxytocin on human interactions. ‘For eight years, it
was quite a lonesome field,’ Heinrichs recalls. ‘Now, everyone is interested.’ These
follow-up studies have shown that after a sniff of the hormone, people become
more charitable, better at reading emotions on others’ faces and at communicating
constructively in arguments. Together, the results fuelled the view that oxytocin
universally enhanced the positive aspects of our social nature.
C
Then, after a few years, contrasting findings began to emerge. Simone Shamay-
Tsoory at the University of Haifa, Israel, found that when volunteers played a
competitive game, those who inhaled the hormone showed more pleasure when
they beat other players, and felt more envy when others won. What’s more,
administering oxytocin also has sharply contrasting outcomes depending on a
person’s disposition. Jennifer Bartz from Mount Sinai School of Medicine, New
York, found that it improves people’s ability to read emotions, but only if they are
not very socially adept to begin with. Her research also shows that oxytocin in fact
reduces cooperation in subjects who are particularly anxious or sensitive
to rejection.
42

Reading
D
Another discovery is that oxytocin’s effects vary depending on who we are
interacting with. Studies conducted by Carolyn DeClerck of the University of
Antwerp, Belgium, revealed that people who had received a dose of oxytocin
actually became less cooperative when dealing with complete strangers.
Meanwhile, Carsten De Dreu at the University of Amsterdam in the Netherlands
discovered that volunteers given oxytocin showed favouritism: Dutch men became
quicker to associate positive words with Dutch names than with foreign ones,
for example. According to De Dreu, oxytocin drives people to care for those in
their social circles and defend them from outside dangers. So, it appears that
oxytocin strengthens biases, rather than promoting general goodwill, as was
previously thought.
E
There were signs of these subtleties from the start. Bartz has recently shown that
in almost half of the existing research results, oxytocin influenced only certain
individuals or in certain circumstances. Where once researchers took no notice
of such findings, now a more nuanced understanding of oxytocin’s effects is
propelling investigations down new lines. To Bartz, the key to understanding what
the hormone does lies in pinpointing its core function rather than in cataloguing its
seemingly endless effects. There are several hypotheses which are not mutually
exclusive. Oxytocin could help to reduce anxiety and fear. Or it could simply
motivate people to seek out social connections. She believes that oxytocin acts as
a chemical spotlight that shines on social cues – a shift in posture, a flicker of the
eyes, a dip in the voice – making people more attuned to their social environment.
This would explain why it makes us more likely to look others in the eye and
improves our ability to identify emotions. But it could also make things worse for
people who are overly sensitive or prone to interpreting social cues in the
worst light.
F
Perhaps we should not be surprised that the oxytocin story has become more
perplexing. The hormone is found in everything from octopuses to sheep, and its
evolutionary roots stretch back half a billion years. ‘It’s a very simple and ancient
molecule that has been co-opted for many different functions,’ says Sue Carter at
the University of Illinois, Chicago, USA. ‘It affects primitive parts of the brain like
the amygdala, so it’s going to have many effects on just about everything.’ Bartz
agrees. ‘Oxytocin probably does some very basic things, but once you add our
higher-order thinking and social situations, these basic processes could manifest
in different ways depending on individual differences and context.’

MAKING THE MOST OF TRENDS
Experts from Harvard Business School give advice to managers
Most managers can identify the major trends of the day. But in the course of conducting research
in a number of industries and working directly with companies, we have discovered that
managers often fail to recognize the less obvious but profound ways these trends are influencing
consumers’ aspirations, attitudes, and behaviors. This is especially true of trends that managers
view as peripheral to their core markets.
Many ignore trends in their innovation strategies or adopt a wait-and-see approach and let
competitors take the lead. At a minimum, such responses mean missed profit opportunities. At
the extreme, they can jeopardize a company by ceding to rivals the opportunity to transform the
industry. The purpose of this article is twofold: to spur managers to think more expansively about
how trends could engender new value propositions in their core markets, and to provide some
high-level advice on how to make market research and product development personnel more
adept at analyzing and exploiting trends.
One strategy, known as ‘infuse and augment’, is to design a product or service that retains most
of the attributes and functions of existing products in the category but adds others that address
the needs and desires unleashed by a major trend. A case in point is the Poppy range of handbags,
which the firm Coach created in response to the economic downturn of 2008. The Coach brand
had been a symbol of opulence and luxury for nearly 70 years, and the most obvious reaction
to the downturn would have been to lower prices. However, that would have risked cheapening
the brand’s image. Instead, they initiated a consumer-research project which revealed that
customers were eager to lift themselves and the country out of tough times. Using these insights,
Coach launched the lower-priced Poppy handbags, which were in vibrant colors, and looked
more youthful and playful than conventional Coach products. Creating the sub-brand allowed
Coach to avert an across-the-board price cut. In contrast to the many companies that responded
to the recession by cutting prices, Coach saw the new consumer mindset as an opportunity for
innovation and renewal.
A further example of this strategy was supermarket Tesco’s response to consumers’ growing
concerns about the environment. With that in mind, Tesco, one of the world’s top five retailers,
introduced its Greener Living program, which demonstrates the company’s commitment to
protecting the environment by involving consumers in ways that produce tangible results. For
example, Tesco customers can accumulate points for such activities as reusing bags, recycling
cans and printer cartridges, and buying home-insulation materials. Like points earned on regular
purchases, these green points can be redeemed for cash. Tesco has not abandoned its traditional
retail offerings but augmented its business with these innovations, thereby infusing its value
proposition with a green streak.
46

Reading
A more radical strategy is ‘combine and transcend’. This entails combining aspects of the
product’s existing value proposition with attributes addressing changes arising from a trend, to
create a novel experience – one that may land the company in an entirely new market space.
At first glance, spending resources to incorporate elements of a seemingly irrelevant trend into
one’s core offerings sounds like it’s hardly worthwhile. But consider Nike’s move to integrate the
digital revolution into its reputation for high-performance athletic footwear. In 2006, they teamed
up with technology company Apple to launch Nike+, a digital sports kit comprising a sensor
that attaches to the running shoe and a wireless receiver that connects to the user’s iPod. By
combining Nike’s original value proposition for amateur athletes with one for digital consumers,
the Nike+ sports kit and web interface moved the company from a focus on athletic apparel to a
new plane of engagement with its customers.
A third approach, known as ‘counteract and reaffirm’, involves developing products or services
that stress the values traditionally associated with the category in ways that allow consumers to
oppose – or at least temporarily escape from – the aspects of trends they view as undesirable.
A product that accomplished this is the ME2, a video game created by Canada’s iToys. By
reaffirming the toy category’s association with physical play, the ME2 counteracted some of
the widely perceived negative impacts of digital gaming devices. Like other handheld games,
the device featured a host of exciting interactive games, a full-color LCD screen, and advanced
3D graphics. What set it apart was that it incorporated the traditional physical component
of children’s play: it contained a pedometer, which tracked and awarded points for physical
activity (walking, running, biking, skateboarding, climbing stairs). The child could use the
points to enhance various virtual skills needed for the video game. The ME2, introduced in mid-
2008, catered to kids’ huge desire to play video games while countering the negatives, such as
associations with lack of exercise and obesity.
Once you have gained perspective on how trend-related changes in consumer opinions and
behaviors impact on your category, you can determine which of our three innovation strategies to
pursue. When your category’s basic value proposition continues to be meaningful for consumers
influenced by the trend, the infuse-and-augment strategy will allow you to reinvigorate the
category. If analysis reveals an increasing disparity between your category and consumers’ new
focus, your innovations need to transcend the category to integrate the two worlds. Finally,
if aspects of the category clash with undesired outcomes of a trend, such as associations with
unhealthy lifestyles, there is an opportunity to counteract those changes by reaffirming the core
values of your category.
Trends – technological, economic, environmental, social, or political – that affect how people
perceive the world around them and shape what they expect from products and services present
firms with unique opportunities for growth.

What set it apart was that it incorporated the traditional physical component of children’s play: it contained a pedometer, which tracked and awarded points for physical activity (walking, running, biking, skateboarding, climbing stairs). The child could use the points to enhance various virtual skills needed for the video game. The ME2, introduced in mid-2008, catered to kids’ huge desire to play video games while countering the negatives, such as associations with lack of exercise and obesity.

Once you have gained perspective on how trend-related changes in consumer opinions and behaviors impact on your category, you can determine which of our three innovation strategies to pursue. When your category’s basic value proposition continues to be meaningful for consumers influenced by the trend, the infuse-and-augment strategy will allow you to reinvigorate the category. If analysis reveals an increasing disparity between your category and consumers’ new focus, your innovations need to transcend the category to integrate the two worlds. Finally, if aspects of the category clash with undesired outcomes of a trend, such as associations with unhealthy lifestyles, there is an opportunity to counteract those changes by reaffirming the core values of your category.

Trends – technological, economic, environmental, social, or political – that affect how people perceive the world around them and shape what they expect from products and services present firms with unique opportunities for growth.

readingSections.title: Reading Passage 1
paragraphs: Cinnamon is a sweet, fragrant spice produced from the inner bark of trees of the genus Cinnamomum, which is native to the Indian sub-continent. It was known in biblical times, and is mentioned in several books of the Bible, both as an ingredient that was mixed with oils for anointing people’s bodies, and also as a token indicating friendship among lovers and friends. In ancient Rome, mourners attending funerals burnt cinnamon to create a pleasant scent. Most often, however, the spice found its primary use as an additive to food and drink. In the Middle Ages, Europeans who could afford the spice used it to flavour food, particularly meat, and to impress those around them with their ability to purchase an expensive condiment from the ‘exotic’ East. At a banquet, a host would offer guests a plate with various spices piled upon it as a sign of the wealth at his or her disposal. Cinnamon was also reported to have health benefits, and was thought to cure various ailments, such as indigestion.

Toward the end of the Middle Ages, the European middle classes began to desire the lifestyle of the elite, including their consumption of spices. This led to a growth in demand for cinnamon and other spices. At that time, cinnamon was transported by Arab merchants, who closely guarded the secret of the source of the spice from potential rivals. They took it from India, where it was grown, on camels via an overland route to the Mediterranean. Their journey ended when they reached Alexandria. European traders sailed there to purchase their supply of cinnamon, then brought it back to Venice. The spice then travelled from that great trading city to markets all around Europe. Because the overland trade route allowed for only small quantities of the spice to reach Europe, and because Venice had a virtual monopoly of the trade, the Venetians could set the price of cinnamon exorbitantly high. These prices, coupled with the increasing demand, spurred the search for new routes to Asia by Europeans eager to take part in the spice trade.

Seeking the high profits promised by the cinnamon market, Portuguese traders arrived on the island of Ceylon in the Indian Ocean toward the end of the 15th century. Before Europeans arrived on the island, the state had organized the cultivation of cinnamon. People belonging to the ethnic group called the Salagama would peel the bark off young shoots of the cinnamon plant in the rainy season, when the wet bark was more pliable. During the peeling process, they curled the bark into the ‘stick’ shape still associated with the spice today. The Salagama then gave the finished product to the king as a form of tribute. When the Portuguese arrived, they needed to increase production significantly, and so enslaved many other members of the Ceylonese native population, forcing them to work in cinnamon harvesting. In 1518, the Portuguese built a fort on Ceylon, which enabled them to protect the island, so helping them to develop a monopoly in the cinnamon trade and generate very high profits. In the late 16th century, for example, they enjoyed a tenfold profit when shipping cinnamon over a journey of eight days from Ceylon to India.

When the Dutch arrived off the coast of southern Asia at the very beginning of the 17th century, they set their sights on displacing the Portuguese as kings of cinnamon. The Dutch allied themselves with Kandy, an inland kingdom on Ceylon. In return for payments of elephants and cinnamon, they protected the native king from the Portuguese. By 1640, the Dutch broke the 150-year Portuguese monopoly when they overran and occupied their factories. By 1658, they had permanently expelled the Portuguese from the island, thereby gaining control of the lucrative cinnamon trade. In order to protect their hold on the market, the Dutch, like the Portuguese before them, treated the native inhabitants harshly. Because of the need to boost production and satisfy Europe’s ever-increasing appetite for cinnamon, the Dutch began to alter the harvesting practices of the Ceylonese. Over time, the supply of cinnamon trees on the island became nearly exhausted, due to systematic stripping of the bark. Eventually, the Dutch began cultivating their own cinnamon trees to supplement the diminishing number of wild trees available for use.

Then, in 1796, the English arrived on Ceylon, thereby displacing the Dutch from their control of the cinnamon monopoly. By the middle of the 19th century, production of cinnamon reached 1,000 tons a year, after a lower grade quality of the spice became acceptable to European tastes. By that time, cinnamon was being grown in other parts of the Indian Ocean region and in the West Indies, Brazil, and Guyana. Not only was a monopoly of cinnamon becoming impossible, but the spice trade overall was diminishing in economic potential, and was eventually superseded by the rise of trade in coffee, tea, chocolate, and sugar.

sentences.text: Cinnamon is a sweet, fragrant spice produced from the inner bark of trees of the genus Cinnamomum, which is native to the Indian sub-continent.
sentences.translation: 肉桂是一种气味芬芳、味道甘甜的香料，由樟属树木的内层树皮制成；这类树木原产于印度次大陆。
sentences.structure: 主干是 Cinnamon is a ... spice；produced... 是过去分词短语修饰 spice，of the genus Cinnamomum 修饰 trees，which 从句说明该属植物的原产地。开篇用“是什么—从哪里来”建立物种与商品身份。

sentences.text: It was known in biblical times, and is mentioned in several books of the Bible, both as an ingredient that was mixed with oils for anointing people’s bodies, and also as a token indicating friendship among lovers and friends.
sentences.translation: 早在《圣经》时代，人们就知道肉桂；《圣经》的多卷书中也提到它：它既是与油混合、用来涂抹人体的配料，也被当作爱侣与朋友之间象征友谊的信物。
sentences.structure: and 连接两个并列谓语 was known 与 is mentioned；both as...and also as... 并列肉桂的两种用途。that was mixed... 修饰 ingredient，for anointing... 表用途，indicating... 修饰 token。两种用途从宗教仪式推进到人际象征。

vocabulary.meaning: 肉桂；本句中的 it 回指该词
以油涂抹身体，常带宗教或仪式含义
象征感情或意图的信物

sentences.text: In ancient Rome, mourners attending funerals burnt cinnamon to create a pleasant scent.
sentences.translation: 在古罗马，参加葬礼的哀悼者会焚烧肉桂，以营造怡人的香气。
sentences.structure: 主干是 mourners burnt cinnamon；attending funerals 是现在分词短语修饰 mourners，to create... 表目的。句子把肉桂从文本记载带入具体仪式场景。

vocabulary.meaning: 肉桂；本句作为焚烧产生香气的材料

sentences.text: Most often, however, the spice found its primary use as an additive to food and drink.
sentences.translation: 不过，肉桂最常见的主要用途还是作为食品和饮料的添加物。
sentences.structure: 主干是 the spice found its primary use as...；Most often 与 however 共同把叙述从仪式用途转回日常用途，as an additive 表明它所充当的角色。

sentences.text: In the Middle Ages, Europeans who could afford the spice used it to flavour food, particularly meat, and to impress those around them with their ability to purchase an expensive condiment from the ‘exotic’ East.
sentences.translation: 中世纪时，买得起这种香料的欧洲人用它给食物调味，尤其是肉类；他们还借自己有能力购买来自“异域”东方的昂贵调味品，给周围的人留下深刻印象。
sentences.structure: 主干是 Europeans used it... and to impress...；who could afford... 修饰 Europeans，两个 to 不定式并列说明实用与炫示用途，with their ability... 交代留下印象的手段。引号中的 exotic 暗示欧洲人的异域想象。

vocabulary.meaning: 异域的；带陌生、新奇色彩

sentences.text: At a banquet, a host would offer guests a plate with various spices piled upon it as a sign of the wealth at his or her disposal.
sentences.translation: 在宴会上，主人会给宾客端上一只盘子，盘中堆放着各种香料，以此显示自己可支配的财富。
sentences.structure: 主干是 a host would offer guests a plate；with... 是介词短语修饰 plate，piled upon it 是过去分词短语修饰 spices，as a sign of... 表示展示目的。香料从调味品变成财富的可视化符号。

vocabulary.meaning: 香料；本句复数指宴席上陈列的多种香料

sentences.text: Cinnamon was also reported to have health benefits, and was thought to cure various ailments, such as indigestion.
sentences.translation: 据说肉桂还有益健康，并被认为可以治疗各种病症，例如消化不良。
sentences.structure: 两个被动谓语 was reported 与 was thought 并列；to have 与 to cure 分别承接报道和看法，such as 引出具体病症。被动结构保留了历史说法的距离，并不把疗效写成现代事实。

sentences.text: Toward the end of the Middle Ages, the European middle classes began to desire the lifestyle of the elite, including their consumption of spices.
sentences.translation: 临近中世纪末期，欧洲中产阶层开始向往精英阶层的生活方式，其中也包括他们消费香料的习惯。
sentences.structure: 主干是 the European middle classes began to desire...；Toward... 给时间背景，including... 补充精英生活方式的具体内容。本段由身份模仿引出需求增长。

vocabulary.meaning: 香料；本句用复数概括精英消费品

sentences.text: This led to a growth in demand for cinnamon and other spices.
sentences.translation: 这导致肉桂及其他香料的需求增长。
sentences.structure: 主干是 This led to...；This 回指中产阶层模仿精英消费，a growth in demand 把社会欲望转化为市场结果。

vocabulary.meaning: 香料；本句指肉桂之外的其他香料

sentences.text: At that time, cinnamon was transported by Arab merchants, who closely guarded the secret of the source of the spice from potential rivals.
sentences.translation: 当时，肉桂由阿拉伯商人运输；他们严密守护香料来源的秘密，不让潜在竞争对手得知。
sentences.structure: 主干是 cinnamon was transported...；who 非限制性定语从句补充 merchants 的保密策略，guard...from... 表示防止竞争者获取秘密。供应链信息不透明为欧洲寻找新路线埋下伏笔。

sentences.text: They took it from India, where it was grown, on camels via an overland route to the Mediterranean.
sentences.translation: 他们从印度取得肉桂——肉桂就种植在那里——再用骆驼沿陆路运到地中海。
sentences.structure: 主干是 They took it from India...to the Mediterranean；where 从句说明产地，on camels 表运输工具，via an overland route 表路线。多个介词短语依次画出供应链。

vocabulary.meaning: 肉桂；本句中的 it 回指前句的 cinnamon
骆驼；本句复数作运输工具

sentences.text: Their journey ended when they reached Alexandria.
sentences.translation: 他们抵达亚历山大港时，这段旅程便告结束。
sentences.structure: 主干是 Their journey ended；when 从句说明终点时刻。短句把印度至地中海的陆路运输落在一个明确节点上。

vocabulary.meaning: 旅程；本句指陆路运输过程

sentences.text: European traders sailed there to purchase their supply of cinnamon, then brought it back to Venice.
sentences.translation: 欧洲商人航行到那里采购肉桂货源，然后把肉桂运回威尼斯。
sentences.structure: 主干是 traders sailed...then brought...；to purchase 表航行目的，there 回指 Alexandria，it 回指 cinnamon。句子接续陆路之后的海运环节。

sentences.text: The spice then travelled from that great trading city to markets all around Europe.
sentences.translation: 随后，这种香料从那座重要的贸易城市流向欧洲各地的市场。
sentences.structure: 主干是 The spice travelled from...to...；that great trading city 回指 Venice，空间路径把威尼斯写成欧洲分销枢纽。

sentences.text: Because the overland trade route allowed for only small quantities of the spice to reach Europe, and because Venice had a virtual monopoly of the trade, the Venetians could set the price of cinnamon exorbitantly high.
sentences.translation: 由于陆路贸易路线只能让少量香料抵达欧洲，加之威尼斯实际上垄断了这项贸易，威尼斯人便能把肉桂价格定得高得惊人。
sentences.structure: 两个 because 从句并列给出“供给少”和“垄断”两项原因；主句 the Venetians could set... 写定价结果。allow for 在这里表示容许某种数量通过，不是“考虑到”。

vocabulary.meaning: 香料；本句指进入欧洲的肉桂
高得离谱地；过分昂贵地

sentences.text: These prices, coupled with the increasing demand, spurred the search for new routes to Asia by Europeans eager to take part in the spice trade.
sentences.translation: 这样的高价，再加上不断增长的需求，推动了欧洲人寻找通往亚洲的新路线；他们迫切希望参与香料贸易。
sentences.structure: 主干是 These prices spurred the search；coupled with... 是过去分词插入语补充共同原因，by Europeans 说明寻找者，eager... 修饰 Europeans。价格与需求共同把贸易史推向航海扩张。

sentences.text: Seeking the high profits promised by the cinnamon market, Portuguese traders arrived on the island of Ceylon in the Indian Ocean toward the end of the 15th century.
sentences.translation: 为了追逐肉桂市场所许诺的高额利润，葡萄牙商人在15世纪末来到印度洋的锡兰岛。
sentences.structure: Seeking... 是现在分词短语表示动机，promised by... 修饰 profits；主干 Portuguese traders arrived...。利润诱因把欧洲人的“寻找路线”落实为抵达产地。

vocabulary.meaning: 贸易商；本句指葡萄牙商人

sentences.text: Before Europeans arrived on the island, the state had organized the cultivation of cinnamon.
sentences.translation: 欧洲人抵达该岛之前，当地政权已经组织起肉桂种植。
sentences.structure: Before 从句给时间界线；主句用过去完成时 had organized，强调欧洲人到来前已有制度化生产。

vocabulary.meaning: 国家或政权；本句指当地统治机构

sentences.text: People belonging to the ethnic group called the Salagama would peel the bark off young shoots of the cinnamon plant in the rainy season, when the wet bark was more pliable.
sentences.translation: 属于萨拉伽马族群的人会在雨季从肉桂植株的嫩枝上剥下树皮，因为那时湿润的树皮更柔韧易弯。
sentences.structure: 主干是 People would peel...；belonging... 与 called... 逐层修饰 People 和 ethnic group，when 从句说明选择雨季的原因。would 表过去的惯常做法。

sentences.text: During the peeling process, they curled the bark into the ‘stick’ shape still associated with the spice today.
sentences.translation: 在剥皮过程中，他们把树皮卷成“棒状”；直到今天，人们仍把这种形状与肉桂联系在一起。
sentences.structure: 主干是 they curled the bark into...；still associated... 是过去分词短语修饰 shape。句子解释肉桂棒的外形如何由加工动作形成，并连接古今。

vocabulary.meaning: 树皮；本句再次指被加工的原料

sentences.text: The Salagama then gave the finished product to the king as a form of tribute.
sentences.translation: 随后，萨拉伽马人把制成品交给国王，作为一种贡品。
sentences.structure: 主干是 The Salagama gave the finished product to the king；as a form of tribute 说明交付的制度性质，从生产流程转向权力关系。

sentences.text: When the Portuguese arrived, they needed to increase production significantly, and so enslaved many other members of the Ceylonese native population, forcing them to work in cinnamon harvesting.
sentences.translation: 葡萄牙人到来后，需要大幅提高产量，于是奴役了许多其他锡兰原住民，强迫他们从事肉桂采收。
sentences.structure: When 从句给时间背景；主句并列 needed 与 enslaved，and so 明示因果；forcing... 是现在分词短语补充奴役的结果。句子把利润扩张与强制劳动直接连接。

sentences.text: In 1518, the Portuguese built a fort on Ceylon, which enabled them to protect the island, so helping them to develop a monopoly in the cinnamon trade and generate very high profits.
sentences.translation: 1518年，葡萄牙人在锡兰修建了一座堡垒；这使他们能够保护该岛，进而帮助他们在肉桂贸易中建立垄断并获取极高利润。
sentences.structure: 主干是 the Portuguese built a fort；which 从句说明堡垒的功能，so helping... 表由此产生的进一步结果，develop 与 generate 并列。句子写军事设施如何转化为市场控制。

vocabulary.meaning: 葡萄牙人；本句为修建堡垒并建立垄断的一方

sentences.text: In the late 16th century, for example, they enjoyed a tenfold profit when shipping cinnamon over a journey of eight days from Ceylon to India.
sentences.translation: 例如，在16世纪后期，他们把肉桂从锡兰运往印度，八天航程便能获得十倍利润。
sentences.structure: 主干是 they enjoyed a tenfold profit；when shipping... 是省略主语的时间状语，over a journey of eight days 补充航程长度。tenfold 用一个数字压缩出贸易暴利。

vocabulary.meaning: 利润；本句再次写贸易收益
旅程；本句指八天运输航程

sentences.text: When the Dutch arrived off the coast of southern Asia at the very beginning of the 17th century, they set their sights on displacing the Portuguese as kings of cinnamon.
sentences.translation: 17世纪刚开始时，荷兰人抵达南亚近海，便立志取代葡萄牙人，成为肉桂贸易的霸主。
sentences.structure: When 从句给出新竞争者登场的时间与地点；主干 they set their sights on...，displacing... 是介词 on 的宾语，as kings of cinnamon 写取代后的目标身份。该比喻把商业竞争写成争夺王位。

vocabulary.meaning: 肉桂；本句代指肉桂贸易

sentences.text: The Dutch allied themselves with Kandy, an inland kingdom on Ceylon.
sentences.translation: 荷兰人与康提结盟；康提是锡兰的一个内陆王国。
sentences.structure: 主干是 The Dutch allied themselves with Kandy；逗号后的 an inland kingdom... 是同位语解释 Kandy。短句交代荷兰挑战葡萄牙的本地联盟。

sentences.text: In return for payments of elephants and cinnamon, they protected the native king from the Portuguese.
sentences.translation: 作为获得大象和肉桂报酬的回报，他们保护当地国王免受葡萄牙人侵害。
sentences.structure: In return for... 前置说明交换条件；主干 they protected the native king from...。句子揭示联盟是一项物资与军事保护的交易。

vocabulary.meaning: 葡萄牙人；本句为保护所针对的一方

sentences.text: By 1640, the Dutch broke the 150-year Portuguese monopoly when they overran and occupied their factories.
sentences.translation: 到1640年，荷兰人攻占葡萄牙人的工厂，打破了葡萄牙长达150年的垄断。
sentences.structure: 主干是 the Dutch broke...monopoly；when 从句说明打破垄断的具体行动，overran 与 occupied 并列。时间数字突出垄断持续之久。

vocabulary.meaning: 葡萄牙的；本句修饰 monopoly

sentences.text: By 1658, they had permanently expelled the Portuguese from the island, thereby gaining control of the lucrative cinnamon trade.
sentences.translation: 到1658年，他们已经把葡萄牙人永久逐出该岛，从而控制了利润丰厚的肉桂贸易。
sentences.structure: 主句用过去完成时 had expelled 表示到1658年已完成；thereby gaining... 是现在分词结果状语，说明驱逐带来的贸易控制。

sentences.text: In order to protect their hold on the market, the Dutch, like the Portuguese before them, treated the native inhabitants harshly.
sentences.translation: 为了保住对市场的控制，荷兰人像此前的葡萄牙人一样，残酷对待当地居民。
sentences.structure: In order to... 表目的；the Dutch 是主语，like... 是插入比较，主干落在 treated...harshly。比较结构强调统治者更换，但压迫方式延续。

sentences.text: Because of the need to boost production and satisfy Europe’s ever-increasing appetite for cinnamon, the Dutch began to alter the harvesting practices of the Ceylonese.
sentences.translation: 由于需要提高产量并满足欧洲对肉桂日益增长的强烈需求，荷兰人开始改变锡兰人的采收方式。
sentences.structure: Because of... 给出原因，其中 boost 与 satisfy 并列；主干 the Dutch began to alter...。appetite 把市场需求人格化为越吃越大的胃口。

vocabulary.meaning: 对……的强烈需求；字面义为食欲

sentences.text: Over time, the supply of cinnamon trees on the island became nearly exhausted, due to systematic stripping of the bark.
sentences.translation: 随着时间推移，由于持续而系统地剥取树皮，岛上的肉桂树资源几乎枯竭。
sentences.structure: 主干是 the supply...became nearly exhausted；Over time 写渐变过程，due to... 给直接原因。被动式 exhausted 把生产扩张的生态后果放到句子中心。

sentences.text: Eventually, the Dutch began cultivating their own cinnamon trees to supplement the diminishing number of wild trees available for use.
sentences.translation: 最终，荷兰人开始自行栽培肉桂树，以补充数量日益减少、可供利用的野生树木。
sentences.structure: 主干是 the Dutch began cultivating...；to supplement... 表目的，diminishing 与 available for use 都修饰 wild trees。此句写资源枯竭迫使垄断者转向人工栽培。

sentences.text: Then, in 1796, the English arrived on Ceylon, thereby displacing the Dutch from their control of the cinnamon monopoly.
sentences.translation: 随后在1796年，英国人抵达锡兰，从而取代荷兰人，夺走了他们对肉桂垄断贸易的控制。

readingSections.title: Reading Passage 2
readingSections.subtitle: The positive and negative effects of the chemical known as the ‘love hormone’
paragraphs: Oxytocin is a chemical, a hormone produced in the pituitary gland in the brain. It was through various studies focusing on animals that scientists first became aware of the influence of oxytocin. They discovered that it helps reinforce the bonds between prairie voles, which mate for life, and triggers the motherly behaviour that sheep show towards their newborn lambs. It is also released by women in childbirth, strengthening the attachment between mother and baby. Few chemicals have as positive a reputation as oxytocin, which is sometimes referred to as the ‘love hormone’. One sniff of it can, it is claimed, make a person more trusting, empathetic, generous and cooperative. It is time, however, to revise this wholly optimistic view. A new wave of studies has shown that its effects vary greatly depending on the person and the circumstances, and it can impact on our social interactions for worse as well as for better.

Oxytocin’s role in human behaviour first emerged in 2005. In a groundbreaking experiment, Markus Heinrichs and his colleagues at the University of Freiburg, Germany, asked volunteers to do an activity in which they could invest money with an anonymous person who was not guaranteed to be honest. The team found that participants who had sniffed oxytocin via a nasal spray beforehand invested more money than those who received a placebo instead. The study was the start of research into the effects of oxytocin on human interactions. ‘For eight years, it was quite a lonesome field,’ Heinrichs recalls. ‘Now, everyone is interested.’ These follow-up studies have shown that after a sniff of the hormone, people become more charitable, better at reading emotions on others’ faces and at communicating constructively in arguments. Together, the results fuelled the view that oxytocin universally enhanced the positive aspects of our social nature.

Then, after a few years, contrasting findings began to emerge. Simone Shamay-Tsoory at the University of Haifa, Israel, found that when volunteers played a competitive game, those who inhaled the hormone showed more pleasure when they beat other players, and felt more envy when others won. What’s more, administering oxytocin also has sharply contrasting outcomes depending on a person’s disposition. Jennifer Bartz from Mount Sinai School of Medicine, New York, found that it improves people’s ability to read emotions, but only if they are not very socially adept to begin with. Her research also shows that oxytocin in fact reduces cooperation in subjects who are particularly anxious or sensitive to rejection.

Another discovery is that oxytocin’s effects vary depending on who we are interacting with. Studies conducted by Carolyn DeClerck of the University of Antwerp, Belgium, revealed that people who had received a dose of oxytocin actually became less cooperative when dealing with complete strangers. Meanwhile, Carsten De Dreu at the University of Amsterdam in the Netherlands discovered that volunteers given oxytocin showed favouritism: Dutch men became quicker to associate positive words with Dutch names than with foreign ones, for example. According to De Dreu, oxytocin drives people to care for those in their social circles and defend them from outside dangers. So, it appears that oxytocin strengthens biases, rather than promoting general goodwill, as was previously thought.

There were signs of these subtleties from the start. Bartz has recently shown that in almost half of the existing research results, oxytocin influenced only certain individuals or in certain circumstances. Where once researchers took no notice of such findings, now a more nuanced understanding of oxytocin’s effects is propelling investigations down new lines. To Bartz, the key to understanding what the hormone does lies in pinpointing its core function rather than in cataloguing its seemingly endless effects. There are several hypotheses which are not mutually exclusive. Oxytocin could help to reduce anxiety and fear. Or it could simply motivate people to seek out social connections. She believes that oxytocin acts as a chemical spotlight that shines on social cues – a shift in posture, a flicker of the eyes, a dip in the voice – making people more attuned to their social environment. This would explain why it makes us more likely to look others in the eye and improves our ability to identify emotions. But it could also make things worse for people who are overly sensitive or prone to interpreting social cues in the worst light.

Perhaps we should not be surprised that the oxytocin story has become more perplexing. The hormone is found in everything from octopuses to sheep, and its evolutionary roots stretch back half a billion years. ‘It’s a very simple and ancient molecule that has been co-opted for many different functions,’ says Sue Carter at the University of Illinois, Chicago, USA. ‘It affects primitive parts of the brain like the amygdala, so it’s going to have many effects on just about everything.’ Bartz agrees. ‘Oxytocin probably does some very basic things, but once you add our higher-order thinking and social situations, these basic processes could manifest in different ways depending on individual differences and context.’

readingSections.title: Reading Passage 3
readingSections.subtitle: Experts from Harvard Business School give advice to managers
paragraphs: Most managers can identify the major trends of the day. But in the course of conducting research in a number of industries and working directly with companies, we have discovered that managers often fail to recognize the less obvious but profound ways these trends are influencing consumers’ aspirations, attitudes, and behaviors. This is especially true of trends that managers view as peripheral to their core markets.

Many ignore trends in their innovation strategies or adopt a wait-and-see approach and let competitors take the lead. At a minimum, such responses mean missed profit opportunities. At the extreme, they can jeopardize a company by ceding to rivals the opportunity to transform the industry. The purpose of this article is twofold: to spur managers to think more expansively about how trends could engender new value propositions in their core markets, and to provide some high-level advice on how to make market research and product development personnel more adept at analyzing and exploiting trends.

One strategy, known as ‘infuse and augment’, is to design a product or service that retains most of the attributes and functions of existing products in the category but adds others that address the needs and desires unleashed by a major trend. A case in point is the Poppy range of handbags, which the firm Coach created in response to the economic downturn of 2008. The Coach brand had been a symbol of opulence and luxury for nearly 70 years, and the most obvious reaction to the downturn would have been to lower prices. However, that would have risked cheapening the brand’s image. Instead, they initiated a consumer-research project which revealed that customers were eager to lift themselves and the country out of tough times. Using these insights, Coach launched the lower-priced Poppy handbags, which were in vibrant colors, and looked more youthful and playful than conventional Coach products. Creating the sub-brand allowed Coach to avert an across-the-board price cut. In contrast to the many companies that responded to the recession by cutting prices, Coach saw the new consumer mindset as an opportunity for innovation and renewal.

A further example of this strategy was supermarket Tesco’s response to consumers’ growing concerns about the environment. With that in mind, Tesco, one of the world’s top five retailers, introduced its Greener Living program, which demonstrates the company’s commitment to protecting the environment by involving consumers in ways that produce tangible results. For example, Tesco customers can accumulate points for such activities as reusing bags, recycling cans and printer cartridges, and buying home-insulation materials. Like points earned on regular purchases, these green points can be redeemed for cash. Tesco has not abandoned its traditional retail offerings but augmented its business with these innovations, thereby infusing its value proposition with a green streak.

A more radical strategy is ‘combine and transcend’. This entails combining aspects of the product’s existing value proposition with attributes addressing changes arising from a trend, to create a novel experience – one that may land the company in an entirely new market space. At first glance, spending resources to incorporate elements of a seemingly irrelevant trend into one’s core offerings sounds like it’s hardly worthwhile. But consider Nike’s move to integrate the digital revolution into its reputation for high-performance athletic footwear. In 2006, they teamed up with technology company Apple to launch Nike+, a digital sports kit comprising a sensor that attaches to the running shoe and a wireless receiver that connects to the user’s iPod. By combining Nike’s original value proposition for amateur athletes with one for digital consumers, the Nike+ sports kit and web interface moved the company from a focus on athletic apparel to a new plane of engagement with its customers.

A third approach, known as ‘counteract and reaffirm’, involves developing products or services that stress the values traditionally associated with the category in ways that allow consumers to oppose – or at least temporarily escape from – the aspects of trends they view as undesirable. A product that accomplished this is the ME2, a video game created by Canada’s iToys. By reaffirming the toy category’s association with physical play, the ME2 counteracted some of the widely perceived negative impacts of digital gaming devices. Like other handheld games, the device featured a host of exciting interactive games, a full-color LCD screen, and advanced 3D graphics. What set it apart was that it incorporated the traditional physical component of children’s play: it contained a pedometer, which tracked and awarded points for physical activity (walking, running, biking, skateboarding, climbing stairs). The child could use the points to enhance various virtual skills needed for the video game. The ME2, introduced in mid-2008, catered to kids’ huge desire to play video games while countering the negatives, such as associations with lack of exercise and obesity.

Once you have gained perspective on how trend-related changes in consumer opinions and behaviors impact on your category, you can determine which of our three innovation strategies to pursue. When your category’s basic value proposition continues to be meaningful for consumers influenced by the trend, the infuse-and-augment strategy will allow you to reinvigorate the category. If analysis reveals an increasing disparity between your category and consumers’ new focus, your innovations need to transcend the category to integrate the two worlds. Finally, if aspects of the category clash with undesired outcomes of a trend, such as associations with unhealthy lifestyles, there is an opportunity to counteract those changes by reaffirming the core values of your category.

Trends – technological, economic, environmental, social, or political – that affect how people perceive the world around them and shape what they expect from products and services present firms with unique opportunities for growth.

questions.prompt: In the first paragraph, the writer says that most managers
questions.promptZh: 在第一段中，作者说大多数管理者……

options.A: fail to spot the key consumer trends of the moment.
options.B: make the mistake of focusing only on the principal consumer trends.
options.C: misinterpret market research data relating to current consumer trends.
options.D: are unaware of the significant impact that trends have on consumers’ lives.

optionTranslations.A: 未能发现当下主要的消费者趋势。
optionTranslations.B: 错误地只关注主要的消费者趋势。
optionTranslations.C: 误解了与当前消费者趋势有关的市场调研数据。
optionTranslations.D: 没有意识到趋势对消费者生活所产生的重大影响。

questions.evidence: managers often fail to recognize the less obvious but profound ways these trends are influencing consumers’ aspirations, attitudes, and behaviors
questions.distractors: A/B confuse identifying major trends with understanding their deeper influence; C invents misinterpretation of data.

questions.prompt: According to the third paragraph, Coach was anxious to
questions.promptZh: 根据第三段，Coach急于……

options.A: follow what some of its competitors were doing.
options.B: maintain its prices throughout its range.
options.C: safeguard its reputation as a manufacturer of luxury goods.
options.D: modify the entire look of its brand to suit the economic climate.

optionTranslations.A: 仿效一些竞争对手的做法。
optionTranslations.B: 维持其所有产品的价格。
optionTranslations.C: 维护其奢侈品制造商的声誉。
optionTranslations.D: 改变整个品牌形象以适应经济环境。

questions.evidence: that would have risked cheapening the brand’s image
questions.distractors: A is contradicted by Coach’s contrast with price-cutters; B says the whole range, whereas a lower-priced sub-brand was launched; D overstates the limited sub-brand change.

questions.prompt: What point is made about Tesco’s Greener Living programme?
questions.promptZh: 关于Tesco的Greener Living计划，文中提出了什么观点？

options.A: It did not require Tesco to modify its core business activities.
options.B: It succeeded in attracting a more eco-conscious clientele.
options.C: Its main aim was to raise consumers’ awareness of environmental issues.
options.D: It was not the first time that Tesco had implemented such an initiative.

optionTranslations.A: 它不要求Tesco改变核心业务活动。
optionTranslations.B: 它成功吸引了环保意识更强的客户群。
optionTranslations.C: 其主要目标是提高消费者对环境问题的认识。
optionTranslations.D: 这并非Tesco首次实施此类举措。

questions.evidence: Tesco has not abandoned its traditional retail offerings but augmented its business with these innovations
questions.distractors: B gives an unreported outcome; C substitutes awareness for tangible participation; D has no supporting comparison with an earlier initiative.

questions.prompt: What does the writer suggest about Nike’s strategy?
questions.promptZh: 作者对Nike的策略有何暗示？

options.A: It was an extremely risky strategy at the time.
options.B: It was a strategy that only a major company could afford to follow.
options.C: It was the type of strategy that would not have been possible in the past.
options.D: It was the kind of strategy which might appear to have few obvious benefits.

optionTranslations.A: 当时这是一项风险极高的策略。
optionTranslations.B: 只有大公司才负担得起这种策略。
optionTranslations.C: 这种策略在过去不可能实现。
optionTranslations.D: 这种策略看起来可能没有多少明显好处。

questions.evidence: sounds like it’s hardly worthwhile. But consider Nike’s move
questions.distractors: A, B and C are not stated; the text specifically frames the move as seemingly hardly worthwhile.

questions.prompt: What was original about the ME2?
questions.promptZh: ME2的创新之处是什么？

options.A: It contained technology that had been developed for the sports industry.
options.B: It appealed to young people who were keen to improve their physical fitness.
options.C: It took advantage of a current trend for video games with colourful 3D graphics.
options.D: It was a handheld game that addressed people’s concerns about unhealthy lifestyles.

optionTranslations.A: 它采用了为体育产业开发的技术。
optionTranslations.B: 它吸引了热衷改善体能的年轻人。
optionTranslations.C: 它利用了彩色3D图像电子游戏的流行趋势。
optionTranslations.D: 它是一款回应人们对不健康生活方式担忧的掌上游戏。

questions.evidence: countering the negatives, such as associations with lack of exercise and obesity
questions.distractors: A gives an unsupported origin for the pedometer; B mistakes the mechanism for users’ motive; C describes a conventional feature, not what set ME2 apart.

questions.prompt: It turned the notion that its products could have harmful effects to its own advantage.
questions.promptZh: 它把其产品可能产生有害影响的观念转化成了自身优势。
questions.evidence: the ME2 counteracted some of the widely perceived negative impacts of digital gaming devices
questions.distractors: Coach addresses recession, Tesco environmental concern, and Nike the digital revolution; only iToys directly turns gaming’s unhealthy associations into a differentiator.

questions.prompt: It extended its offering by collaborating with another manufacturer.
questions.promptZh: 它通过与另一家制造商合作扩展了自身产品。
questions.evidence: they teamed up with technology company Apple to launch Nike+
questions.distractors: No partnership with another manufacturer is stated for Coach, Tesco or iToys.

questions.prompt: It implemented an incentive scheme to demonstrate its corporate social responsibility.
questions.promptZh: 它实施了一项激励计划来体现企业社会责任。
questions.evidence: Tesco customers can accumulate points ... these green points can be redeemed for cash
questions.distractors: The other companies launch products; only Tesco rewards environmentally helpful customer actions.

questions.prompt: It discovered that customers had a positive attitude towards dealing with difficult circumstances.
questions.promptZh: 它发现顾客对克服困境持积极态度。
questions.evidence: customers were eager to lift themselves and the country out of tough times
questions.distractors: The finding comes from Coach’s consumer research, not the other three cases.

questions.prompt: It responded to a growing lifestyle trend in an unrelated product sector.
questions.promptZh: 它回应了一个来自无关产品领域、不断增长的生活方式趋势。
questions.evidence: integrate the digital revolution into its reputation for high-performance athletic footwear
questions.distractors: Nike combines footwear with the digital sector; the other examples remain tied to price, retail environmentalism, or gaming’s physical effects.

questions.prompt: It successfully avoided having to charge its customers less for its core products.
questions.promptZh: 它成功避免了不得不降低核心产品售价。
questions.evidence: Creating the sub-brand allowed Coach to avert an across-the-board price cut.
questions.distractors: Only Coach is described as avoiding a price cut across its established range.

questions.prompt: If there are any trend-related changes impacting on your category, you should
questions.promptZh: 如果存在任何影响你所在品类的趋势相关变化，你应该……
questions.evidence: you can determine which of our three innovation strategies to pursue
questions.distractors: A is never advised; C and D apply only after a specific relationship between trend and category is diagnosed.

questions.prompt: If a current trend highlights a negative aspect of your category, you should
questions.promptZh: 如果当前趋势凸显了你所在品类的负面方面，你应该……
questions.evidence: if aspects of the category clash with undesired outcomes of a trend ... counteract those changes by reaffirming the core values
questions.distractors: B is the preliminary general step; D is for disparity, while A is unsupported.

questions.prompt: If the consumers’ new focus has an increasing lack of connection with your offering, you should
questions.promptZh: 如果消费者的新关注点与你的产品越来越脱节，你应该……
questions.evidence: an increasing disparity between your category and consumers’ new focus ... transcend the category to integrate the two worlds
questions.distractors: C applies to undesirable outcomes, B is nonspecific, and A is not a stated recommendation.
